conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’ll be walking with you through a quick check-in that many new moms find helpful. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question tool that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we talk about stays between us unless you give permission to share. My goal is simply to understand how things are going for you right now so we can figure out the best support.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no check-boxes or forms—and you can answer in your own words. When you’re ready, we’ll start.  

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft half-smile, eyes tired]  
Honestly… I can’t remember the last time something really made me laugh. My husband will make a joke—he’s trying—and I’ll try to smile so he doesn’t feel bad, but it feels forced. It’s like the joy is stuck behind a wall. I used to laugh at silly memes or funny shows, and now I’ll scroll past them or turn the TV off because it just feels like too much effort.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shrugs, voice quiet]  
Yeah… I guess that’s the thing—I haven’t. Even when my mom tried to tell me that story about the diaper explosion at church, I just couldn’t find it funny. I wanted to laugh for her, but nothing came out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[eyes drop to my lap, fingers twisting the edge of the baby-blanket]  
Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower. Now I hear myself saying “maybe tomorrow” and then tomorrow feels the same. Yesterday my sister texted about brunch next week; I typed “can’t wait,” then deleted it because the truth is I’m already dreading getting us both dressed. Enjoyment feels… distant, like I remember the word but not the feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up, voice cracks]  
All the time. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it’s because I drank that one cup of coffee—maybe the caffeine got into my milk and made her jittery. When she cried for an hour I was sure I’d missed her sleepy window because I was scrolling on my phone. I tell myself a “good mom” would know her cues better. My head keeps saying everything she struggles with—her spitting up, her fussiness—is somehow my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… it feels like there’s always this low hum of worry in my chest. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly think, “What if she chokes? What if I fall asleep and drop her?” I check her breathing a dozen times a night. Nothing bad is happening, but I can’t shake the fear that something will. Even when she’s napping in her crib, I’m standing at the monitor watching every tiny movement, heart racing, sure something’s wrong even though she looks perfectly fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses a hand to chest]  
Sometimes it hits out of nowhere—like yesterday I was folding her onesies and suddenly my heart was racing so hard I thought I might pass out. I couldn’t name a single real danger in the room, but it felt like something awful was about to happen. The panic only lasts a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and checking every door and window lock, convinced I missed some invisible threat.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly, shoulders sagging]  
Most days, yeah. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, the feeding, the pumping—one big wave after another. I’ll be halfway through folding a basket and she starts crying, so I leave it, then something else piles on. By dinner I’m staring at the stove thinking, “I can’t do one more thing.” I still push through, but it feels like I’m always a step behind, and the mess in my head matches the mess in the living room.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods, eyes red-rimmed]  
That’s been most nights this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t stop replaying everything I think I did wrong—did I burp her long enough, did I strap the car seat tight enough… I stare at the ceiling for an hour, then when I finally drift off she squeaks and I’m wide awake again. Even when she sleeps a four-hour stretch, I wake up at 3 a.m. with this heavy, sick feeling in my chest and can’t get back to sleep. I’m running on maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice small]  
Pretty much every day. I wake up with this weight in my chest that doesn’t really go away. It’s not crying-all-day bad, but it’s like a gray cloud that follows me. I’ll be giving her a bath—something that should feel sweet—and out of nowhere this wave of sadness rolls in and my eyes just start leaking. I end up holding her a little tighter, hoping she can’t sense how down I feel.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. The worst was two nights ago—she wouldn’t latch and I felt this rush of “I’m failing her,” and before I knew it I was sobbing at 2 a.m., trying to stay quiet so I wouldn’t wake my husband. I tell myself it’s just hormones, but the tears keep coming whenever everything feels like too much.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widen]  
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and no matter how low I feel, I couldn’t do that to her or to my family.

You shared openly about feeling persistently down, anxious, and overwhelmed since your baby arrived. Laughing or looking forward to anything feels impossible right now, and you carry a heavy sense of guilt and self-blame. Nights are long with racing thoughts and broken sleep, and sudden waves of panic or tears catch you off guard. While you love your little one and have no thoughts of self-harm, the sadness and worry color most days, leaving you feeling stuck and exhausted.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly reports inability to laugh or find humor in situations that would normally be funny, matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, dreading future events and inability to feel enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>She reports self-blame "all the time," with specific, repeated examples of feeling responsible for the baby's difficulties, matching the highest intensity option "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries without real cause, checking breathing repeatedly and inability to relax even when baby is safe</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>She reports "most days" feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks and mentally behind, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption linked to unhappiness and anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent daily sadness, emotional lability, and tearfulness consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week tied to feeling overwhelmed and inadequate, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 on the EPDS falls well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. The patient endorses <sym>depressed mood most of the day</sym>, <sym>marked loss of interest or pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>diminished ability to think or concentrate</sym>, <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym>, and <sym>insomnia</sym> nearly every day for more than two weeks, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. She also describes recurrent panic attacks and constant intrusive worries consistent with comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Item 10 score of 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression)
3. Discuss benefits and risks of starting an <med>SSRI compatible with breastfeeding</med>
4. Involve partner or family in safety planning and daily support
5. Provide perinatal crisis-line numbers and local support group contacts
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**  
*Date:* [today’s date]  
*Source:* Patient self-report via EPDS-style interview  

**Presenting Symptoms & Observations**  
- Persistent low mood, sadness “pretty much every day”  
- Marked anhedonia (no enjoyment, no laughter, “distant” pleasure)  
- Daily tearfulness, 2 a.m. crying spell this week  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt regarding infant care (“everything she struggles with… is my fault”)  
- Chronic low-grade anxiety with episodic panic (heart racing, breathlessness, no identifiable trigger)  
- Hypervigilant intrusive worries (infant choking, dropping baby, monitor checking ≥12×/night)  
- Initial and middle insomnia linked to rumination; ~4 hrs broken sleep/night  
- Overwhelmed / unable to cope with routine tasks (“one big wave after another”)  

**Screening Significance**  
Responses are consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features; no evidence of psychosis or mania.  

**Safety**  
Denies any thoughts of self-harm; no suicidal ideation voiced. No immediate safety concern identified.  

**Recommendation**  
Continue to full clinical evaluation for postpartum mood & anxiety disorders; consider standardized EPDS scoring and collaborative care planning.
